newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK manufacturing grows despite pound's might.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK manufacturing grows despite pound's might.

text.p: British manufacturers chalked up their 13th successive month of growth in June as buoyant domestic demand continued to offset the detrimental effects of a rampant pound, a leading business survey showed on Tuesday.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing Supply's latest purchasing managers index slid to 53.4 from 54.4 in May, as the pace of manufacturing growth eased last month, but any reading above 50 indicates the sector is expanding.
"The main source of new business was the domestic market, with the strength of the pound again reported to have subdued foreign demand," the CIPS said.
The pound, which spurted to a fresh five-year high on Monday, has now climbed about 21 percent against a basket of other major currencies since last August.

The higher it climbs the further exporters' prices are forced up and the harder they find it to sell. But up to now, manufacturers have been bailed out by freely spending British consumers who are pushing retail sales up at a tremendous rate -- about five percent year-on-year.

The CIPS survey, which has developed a good track record in gauging the health of Britain's manufacturers, showed export orders actually rose modestly in June as economic growth in overseas markets picked up.
But its export orders index is well below the levels seen for most of the past year and manufacturers surveyed said the pound was definitely hitting overseas demand.
That should sends a final warning to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown to raise taxes, or risk interest rates going through the roof and worsening the plight of Britain's manufacturers.
Brown will unveil the first Labour budget in nearly 20 years on Wednesday.
The fact the pound is biting into exports while High Street spending grows unfettered suggests personal taxes should be raised to slow consumer demand without unduly hitting the industrial sector.

The problem for Brown is Labour's election manifesto promised not to raise the rates of income tax or broaden the scope of value-added tax. Some economists think the spirit of those pledges will preclude any personal tax increases.

But a failure to rein in the consumer with fiscal measures will leave the newly independent Bank of England little choice but to raise interest rates aggressively which could in turn propel the pound further skywards and undermine manufacturers even more.

"This survey is really a timely reminder that the Chancellor needs to take action to dampen consumer demand and ease the upward pressure on the pound," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"While there are no signs of collapse in industry, there are strong hints here of the damage that might lie ahead, particularly if sterling keeps on rising."
Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, agreed the survey would give some last food for thought for the Chancellor.
"The message from this survey...is that export growth is being affected by the pound and growth in the manufacturing sector is rather anaemic."

But manufacturers are likely to have to cope with more monetary tightening no matter what Brown does even though base rates have been ratcheted up in two quarter-point jumps to 6.5 percent since Labour took power on May 1.

"Although Mr Brown is likely to take action to cool demand...nothing but personal sector tax increases worth perhaps seven billion pounds is likely to prevent the Bank of England's monetary policy committee meeting from pushing up interest rates again shortly," Loynes said.
The consensus is that his budget will produce a net tightening of more like three or four billion. The Bank's monetary policy committee meets next week and will announce its decision on July 10.
